result.summary: KCERA seeks one qualified actuarial firm to audit its cost-sharing defined-benefit pension plan, which covers County of Kern and participating-agency employees and operates independently; Segal Consulting provides actuarial consulting through April 1, 2025. The RFP was issued March 29, 2024; proposals were due by email May 17 before 2:00 p.m. PT, with Board approval and contract commencement scheduled for June 12. Bids must include a not-to-exceed price, separately identifying incidental costs. Proposals may be changed or withdrawn in writing before the deadline; late submissions are rejected. Respondents must promptly report errors; KCERA may issue website addenda or extend the deadline, while unreported errors remain the respondent’s risk. Proposals become KCERA property and are subject to public-records and open-meeting laws; limited portions may be marked confidential, subject to KCERA review and related indemnity obligations. Respondents bear preparation costs and their own taxes; KCERA is tax-exempt. KCERA may discuss or clarify issues with finalists. Submission accepts RFP terms unless objections, proposed revisions, and reasons are specified; KCERA may revise the contract before signing.

result.title: SECTION THREE – ENTITY DESCRIPTION
result.summary: KCERA is an independent California cost-sharing, multiple-employer defined-benefit pension plan established in 1945, serving Kern County and 14 participating agencies. The section describes its governance, membership and financial position, and benefit provisions across five tiers, including eligibility, pension calculations, beneficiary choices, reciprocity, disability and death benefits, COLAs, and supplemental benefits. It explains the seven reserves, reserve balances, actuarial funding and employer/member contribution rules, pension obligation bonds, retiree COLA funding, and GASB disclosures. It also presents actuarial methods and assumptions, assets, liabilities and funded ratio; UAAL amortization periods; statutory valuation requirements and experience studies; and the pension administration data and payroll feeds used for valuations.

nodes.title: 3.1 BACKGROUND INFORMATION
nodes.summary: KCERA is a cost-sharing, multiple-employer defined-benefit pension plan established January 1, 1945, under California’s County Employees Retirement Law of 1937. It provides retirement, disability, death, and survivor benefits to County of Kern employees and participating agencies: Kern County Superior Courts, Kern County Hospital Authority, Berrenda Mesa Water District, Buttonwillow Recreation and Park District, East Kern Cemetery District, Inyokern Community Services District, Kern County Water Agency, Kern Mosquito & Vector Control District, North of the River Sanitation District, San Joaquin Valley Unified Air Pollution Control District, Shafter Recreation and Park District, West Side Cemetery District, West Side Mosquito & Vector Control District, and West Side Recreation and Park District. KCERA is an independent governmental entity, administered by a nine-member Board of Retirement and two alternates; four members are appointed, four elected, and the County Treasurer serves ex officio. Unified valuations and investigations cover the County and 14 agencies. KCERA’s financial statements are referenced in the County’s annual report. As of June 30, 2023, it had approximately 13,940 active and deferred members, 9,156 retirees, and $5.4 billion in fiduciary net position.

nodes.title: 3.2 PLAN INFORMATION AND BENEFIT PROVISIONS
nodes.summary: KCERA provides retirement, disability, death, beneficiary, cost-of-living, and supplemental benefits under fixed formulas adopted or amended from 1968 through PEPRA: Safety Tier I (3% at 50), General Tier I (3% at 60), General Tier II (1.62% at 65), Safety Tier II (2% at 50), and General Tier III (2.5% at 67). Retirement eligibility varies by tier; lifetime pensions depend on age, service, tier, and final compensation (12-month average for pre-2013 members; 36-month average thereafter). Members select among four beneficiary options; vested Tier I–II members may defer benefits, and reciprocity may be established by joining another public system within 180 days. Disability requires five years for non-work-related cases, but no age or service minimum for work-related incapacity. Duty-related deaths may provide lifetime survivor allowances; post-retirement death benefits are $5,000, with continuances depending on circumstances and option. COLA can reach 2.5%. The Board controls non-guaranteed SRBR benefits. Restructured in 2022, the SRBR sets a floor using the higher of a $1.80-per-service-year calculation or the former structure, with annual 2.5% COLA when adequately funded and review triggers above 115% or below 95% funding for two years. A 2002 settlement added a permanent 0.5% COLA.

nodes.title: 3.2 PLAN INFORMATION AND BENEFIT PROVISIONS (intro)
nodes.summary: KCERA provides retirement, disability, death, beneficiary, cost-of-living, and supplemental retirement benefits under a fixed benefit formula adopted by Kern County in 1968. Subsequent formula changes established: Safety Tier I, 3% at 50 (Government Code §31664.1), effective January 1, 2001; General Tier I, 3% at 60 (§31676.17, replacing §31676.14), effective January 1, 2005; General Tier II, 1.62% at 65 (§31676.01), for general members hired on or after October 27, 2007; Safety Tier II, 2% at 50 (§31664), for safety members hired on or after March 27, 2012; and General Tier III, 2.5% at 67, established under PEPRA effective January 1, 2013, for new West Side Recreation and Park District employees who became new members on or after that date.

nodes.title: Service Retirement Benefit
nodes.summary: Eligible employees participate in KCERA. General and Safety Tiers I–II retirement eligibility is age 50 with 10 years’ service, or 30 years for General/20 for Safety regardless of age; General Tier III requires age 52 and five years. Lifetime monthly pensions depend on age, service credit, tier, and final compensation: highest 12-month average of compensation earnable for members before 2013, or highest 36-month average of pensionable compensation for later members. Retirees choose among four beneficiary options; the unmodified allowance continues 60% to a surviving spouse. Vested Tier I–II members may defer benefits after leaving contributions on deposit. Members entering a reciprocal public retirement system within 180 days may establish reciprocity. Pre-retirement death benefits include contributions with interest and salary-based payments; vested or duty-related deaths may provide lifetime survivor allowances. Post-retirement death pays $5,000, with continuances depending on retirement type and option. Disability benefits require five years for nonservice cases, but no age or service minimum for work-related disability. COLA may reach 2.5%. The Board controls non-guaranteed supplemental benefits from the SRBR for retirees, future retirees, and beneficiaries.

nodes.title: Death, Disability, and Retirement Benefits
nodes.summary: For a member who dies in the performance of duty, the spouse receives a lifetime monthly allowance of at least 50% of final average salary; if there is no spouse, eligible children receive it until age 18, or 22 if enrolled full-time in an accredited school. After retirement, a $5,000 death benefit (raised from $3,000 effective January 1, 2015) goes to the designated beneficiary or estate. Under the unmodified option, surviving spouses or minor children receive 60% of the allowance after service- or nonservice-connected disability retirement; after service-connected disability retirement, they receive 100%. Nonservice-connected disability retirement requires five years of service and permanent incapacity, regardless of age. Service-connected disability requires permanent work-related incapacity, with no age or service requirement. Retirees and continuance beneficiaries receive an annual COLA of up to 2%, increased by 0.5% under the Ventura Settlement effective April 1, 2002, for a maximum of 2.5%, depending on inflation.

nodes.title: Supplemental Benefit
nodes.summary: The Board adopted Government Code Section 31618 in 1984 to establish the Supplemental Retiree Benefit Reserve (SRBR), which benefits current and future retirees and beneficiaries. Supplemental benefits are not guaranteed, and the Board determines distributions. In 2022, KCERA restructured the program: each member’s starting (“floor”) benefit was set to the higher of a one-time calculation under the new $1.80-per-year-of-service formula or the former SRBR 1–4 structure. Eligible members receive an annual 2.5% COLA while the SRBR is adequately funded. The Board will consider benefit changes if funding exceeds 115% or falls below 95% for two consecutive years. The restructuring took effect July 1, 2022, and is fully implemented. Separately, a court settlement effective April 1, 2002, granted retirees and beneficiaries a permanent 0.5% COLA, initially funded by a $64.7 million SRBR allocation.

nodes.title: 3.3 RESERVES
nodes.summary: KCERA allocates contributions among seven reserves for retirement funding, COLAs, annuities, supplemental benefits, future COLA contributions, and contingency needs. At June 30, 2023 and 2022, total reserves were $5.595 billion and $5.351 billion; after market-stabilization reserves, fiduciary net position restricted for pensions was $5.387 billion and $5.131 billion. Annual actuarial valuations use the Entry Age Normal method to set employer rates for normal cost and amortization of unfunded or overfunded liabilities, effective 12 months after valuation. The section describes pension obligation bonds issued in 1995 and 2003, differing employer rates by participation class, and member contribution rules based on tier, employer, bargaining unit, and pay. It covers PEPRA and Social Security rate provisions, employer pickups and changing contribution obligations, including Superior Court rates. Retiree COLAs and their funding are described, along with GASB 67 pension-liability disclosures.

nodes.title: 3.3 RESERVES (intro)
nodes.summary: KCERA allocates member and employer contributions, based on actuarial determinations, among seven reserves: Members’ Deposit and Employers’ Advance (retirement funding); Cost-of-Living (retiree and beneficiary increases); Retired Members’ (monthly annuities); Supplemental Retiree Benefit (enhanced non-vested benefits); COLA Contribution (future employer COLA contributions); and Contingency (supplement deficient earnings, meeting the statutory requirement to hold 1%–3% of assets). A table in thousands reports June 30, 2023 and 2022 balances under the five-year smoothed-market valuation method, itemized by member/employer group and reserve. Total reserves were $5,595,428 and $5,351,182; market stabilization reserves were $(208,847) and $(220,053); total fiduciary net position restricted for pension benefits was $5,386,581 and $5,131,129, respectively. The next section is Funding Status and Progress, beginning with Contributions.

nodes.title: Employer Contributions
nodes.summary:
Employer Contributions
Each year, an actuarial valuation is performed for the purpose of determining the funded position of the retirement plan and the employer contributions that are necessary to pay
13Kern County Employees’ Retirement Association Actuarial Audit Services RFP
benefits accruing to KCERA members not otherwise funded by member contributions or investment earnings. The employer contribution rates are actuarially determined by using the Entry Age Normal Actuarial Cost method. The Plan’s employer rates provide for both normal cost and a contribution to amortize any unfunded or overfunded actuarial accrued liabilities. Contribution rates determined in each actuarial valuation (as of June 30) apply to the fiscal year beginning 12 months after the valuation date.

nodes.title: Pension Obligation Bonds
nodes.summary: Kern County issued pension obligation bonds in 1995 and 2003, contributing $224.5 million and $285.1 million to the Plan; special districts did not participate, so contribution rates differ by participation class to fund unfunded liabilities. Member contributions are pre-tax payroll deductions under IRS Code Section 414(h)(2), based on base and compensable special pay, with rates determined by entry age, actuarial benefits, tier, employer, and bargaining unit; some safety units have flat rates. PEPRA members entering on or after January 1, 2013, pay 50% of normal cost plus COLA. Social Security-covered members receive a one-third rate reduction on the first $350 of monthly salary. Employer pickups and subsequent payment requirements vary by MOU, hire date, employer, and special-district election; Superior Court contribution rates rose from 2.5% to 3%, 3.5%, then 4% between 2011 and 2012. A COLA of up to 2% for retirees and continuance beneficiaries was adopted effective April 1, 1973.

nodes.title: Member Contributions
nodes.summary: Employer rates are determined using Entry Age Normal, covering normal cost and amortization of unfunded/overfunded liabilities; June 30 valuation rates take effect 12 months later. Kern County issued pension obligation bonds in 1995 and 2003, contributing $224.5 million and $285.1 million; districts did not participate, so employer rates differ by participation class. Pre-tax member contributions depend on tier, employer, bargaining unit, entry age, and benefits, apply to base and compensable special pay, and may be flat for safety units. PEPRA members (from 2013) pay 50% of normal cost plus COLA; Social Security members pay reduced rates on the first $350 monthly salary. The text details employer pickups and changing employee contribution obligations, including court and special-district rates. Retiree COLA rose from up to 2% (1973) to 2.5% (2002); funding shifted from fund balance to employer contributions, with excess earnings used first and $64.7 million from SRBR funding the increase. GASB 67 disclosures cover net pension liability, discount-rate sensitivity, liability changes, assumptions/methods, and contributions.

nodes.title: 3.4 ACTUARIAL INFORMATION
nodes.summary: KCERA uses Segal Consulting for annual actuarial valuations; at June 30, 2023, actuarial assets were $5.436 billion, accrued liability was $7.919 billion, and the funded ratio was 68.65%. The valuation uses the entry-age method, five-year smoothed market assets, a 7.00% investment return, 3.00% salary growth, 2.50% inflation, and 3.00% cost-of-living inflation. UAAL amortization uses level-percent-of-pay methods, with specified closed periods for existing UAAL, experience or assumption changes, plan amendments, and retirement incentives. State law requires valuations at least every three years and provides for Board recommendations on interest, contribution, and appropriation rates; KCERA values annually and conducts triennial assumption experience studies. Its 2019–2022 experience analysis was completed in May 2023. Actuarial data comes from CPAS, a custom pension administration system holding records for active, deferred, retired, terminated, and nonparticipating members. It receives biweekly sponsor payroll feeds covering membership changes, salaries, contributions, and related data.

result.title: SECTION FIVE – MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS
result.summary: The RFP requires an actuarial audit firm to provide valuations, experience investigations, audits, and pension consulting, and to perform contract services skillfully under applicable professional and enrolled-actuary standards. The responsible actuary must meet federal enrollment requirements and be a Fellow of the Society of Actuaries. Supporting actuaries must be Fellows, enrolled actuaries, or have at least ten years of pension consulting experience. The lead actuary must have at least ten years’ experience in pension consulting, experience analysis, valuations, and actuarial audits for multi-employer public retirement systems. The firm must disclose all potential conflicts of interest.

result.summary: Proposals must follow the prescribed format, address every required item, use the specified section titles, and include hard-copy submissions of the cover letter and proposal, signed Guarantees and Warranties forms, and the Dollar Cost Bid. KCERA may allow five business days to correct minor omissions after notification; major omissions, including missing prices, result in disqualification. The signed cover letter must identify the RFP, confirm capability and willingness to provide services under its terms, and include proof of signatory authority. The proposal must detail the approach and sequence for completing the scope, required KCERA staff involvement, and the Exhibit C questionnaire; explain quality, cost, timeliness, and confidentiality controls; provide a fixed fee; state all cost assumptions (with no others recognized); and identify all exceptions (only those listed here will be considered). Include at least three similar-service references, including applicable California 1937 Act pension funds, with contact details; key team members’ roles, workload, client counts, team tenure, experience, and qualifications; and sample actuarial audit valuation reports.

result.title: EXHIBIT B – SCOPE OF SERVICES
result.summary: KCERA seeks one actuarial firm to audit the 2019–2022 experience study and June 30, 2023 valuation. For the experience-study peer review, the auditor will consult KCERA staff and its consulting actuary, assess census data quality, sufficiency and assumptions, review recommended economic and non-economic assumptions, and reconcile differences in findings, methods, rates and adjustments. Data from the prior four valuations will be provided. Results should be shared before the consulting actuary completes the June 30, 2024 valuation. The auditor will also independently reproduce the June 30, 2023 valuation, including SRBR and GASB 67, using supplied raw and scrubbed data and the consulting actuary’s assumptions, methods and funding method, without relying on its work. The auditor will assess data adequacy, evaluate results, reconcile discrepancies, and communicate findings before the June 30, 2024 valuation.

result.title: EXHIBIT C – QUESTIONNAIRE
result.summary: The questionnaire seeks firm contact and organizational information, including ownership, affiliates, leadership, offices and staffing, KCERA service location, competitive strengths, litigation or regulatory history, conflicts and safeguards, Segal relationships, professional ties to KCERA, and gifts or hospitality. It requests Primary and Secondary Actuary qualifications, experience, KCERA roles and time, client workloads, audit histories, outside affiliations, staff turnover details, and succession plans. Firms must explain Exhibit B service methodology, timelines, assumptions and cost-method selection, interest-rate advice, quality controls, and provide a recent audit report (Appendix C). Experience questions cover audit-client totals, public pension clients and plan details, specified references, threatened or defaulted contracts, and external audits of the firm’s work. Resource questions address subcontracting, legal expertise, insurance coverage and carriers, client-satisfaction monitoring, and public-fund resources. Fee questions cover fee determination, billing timing, and inclusion of administrative, third-party, travel, and other costs. Required organization charts are Appendices A and B.

nodes.title: Organization and Ownership
nodes.summary: The questionnaire requests the firm’s response date and contact details; background, formation, ownership and ownership changes, affiliates/joint ventures, executive succession, and the strategic and revenue significance of actuarial consulting. It requires Appendix A ownership/interrelationship and Appendix B actuarial-group/staff organization charts; office locations, functions, professional counts, and the office responsible for KCERA; and the firm’s competitive advantages and case for selection. It asks about relevant litigation or proceedings over five years, disputes with KCERA, and regulatory censures or fines over ten years. It also covers potential conflicts involving non-actuarial affiliates and safeguards, business relationships with Segal Consulting or Segal Group, professional relationships with KCERA board members, staff, or plan sponsors, and any gifts, travel, entertainment, or meals provided to KCERA board members or staff during the past year.

nodes.title: Actuarial Services Staffing
nodes.summary: The section requests information about actuarial consulting staffing: the number of actuaries employed; a profile of the Primary and Secondary Actuaries assigned to KCERA, including names, titles, responsibilities and time allocations, experience, tenure, degrees and designations and awarding institutions, and publications; how long they have worked together; and their actuarial audit assignments over the past five years, with report dates, roles, and client names and plan membership sizes. It asks each actuary’s role in KCERA services, current client counts and whether clients receive general actuarial or audit services, and details of any potential conflicts from outside affiliations. It also requests discussion of the causes and effects of five years of staff turnover and a table of departed professionals with departure dates, names, titles, responsibilities, firm tenure, reasons for leaving, and replacements. Finally, it asks whether the firm has a transition plan for sudden departures of key professionals and to describe it.

nodes.title: Methodology
nodes.summary: The section requests a description of the methodology for the services in Exhibit B and a project timeline covering key stages, required input dates from KCERA or its actuary, and planned staff meetings at KCERA’s office. It also asks for the firm’s approach to selecting a public pension fund actuarial cost method, developing actuarial assumptions other than the interest rate, and formulating the interest rate assumption, including how the approach varies by client and when KCERA should change its rate. Firms must describe quality-control, monitoring, and review processes for actuarial audit reports and recommendations, and include as Appendix C a recent actuarial audit report prepared for an existing client.

nodes.title: Relevant Experience
nodes.summary: The RFP requests actuarial-audit experience information: annual totals from 2020–2023 for all relevant audit clients and public pension plan audit clients; current public pension clients’ names, initial contract year, assets and membership as of June 30, 2023, and identification of multi-employer plans; and contact details for client references covering recent actuarial audits, terminated and longest-running full-service consulting contracts, a qualifying multi-employer plan, a client assigned to the proposed Primary Actuary for at least two years, and the Primary Actuary’s most recent audit. It also asks whether any client gave notice within five years of contract default or risk to continuation, with the client, date, reasons and resolution/status, and whether another actuarial firm audited the firm’s consulting products, including the number of audits and any resulting changes to valuation results, assumptions or cost methods.

key_items: W I T N E S S E T H:
result.summary: Draft 2024 agreement between KCERA’s Board of Retirement and a selected actuarial firm, with party, dates, fees, and other details left blank. It requires a peer review of the 2019–2022 experience study and an independent parallel audit of the June 30, 2023 valuation, including data and assumptions review, discrepancy reconciliation, coordination with KCERA staff and its consulting actuary, and timely communication of findings. Reports are due within six months; the actuary provides a digital final report and attends up to two meetings without extra charge. The Board supplies data and pays within a maximum amount. Terms address supervision, confidentiality, incorporated documents and precedence, term and termination, representations, assignment, independent-contractor status, indemnity, insurance, document ownership, notices, conflicts, public-records disclosure, remedies, severability, legal compliance, interpretation, timing, counterparts, nondiscrimination, record audits and retention, non-collusion, signature authority, and exclusion of third-party rights. California law applies, with venue in Kern County.
